opener.heading: Week 24: Water Safety & Swimming Fun 🏊
about: Seven days of water, and each one hands Azlyn one thing she can do in it. On Friday she works out what air does inside a capped bottle, then tapes six of them to a teddy until his chin stays clear. Sunday she runs a pool from a lifeguard chair, whistle on a wool loop round her wrist, and throws a rolled towel to a teddy in trouble at the deep end. Monday she pulls that teddy in with a broom, a wet towel and a bottle on a line, feet on dry ground the whole hour. Each day puts the same question in front of her in a new shape: what do you do when somebody is in the water?

No holiday lands in this week. Tuesday's pool trip sits in the middle of it and the days before it all feed in, so she draws the starfish in chalk on the patio before she ever lies back in water, she blows the bubbles in a bowl on the kitchen table, and she packs the swim bag herself against a picture list she drew. Thursday she takes five tests in the kiddie pool and signs a diploma that says in her own words what she can do. Three things outlast the week: the rules sign by the back door, the card with her full name and address taped up by the phone, and the diploma on the fridge. The pool comes out on Friday morning and it is up all week. Kreston is twelve months and on his feet, so it goes over onto the grass at the end of every water day, and by Wednesday the tipping out is Azlyn's job.
azlyn: Floating on her back. Ears down in the water, chin at the sky, tummy up, held for one counted minute with your hand flat under her back.
Bubbles out through her mouth. Chin resting on the water, mouth under, humming out, learned in a warm bowl on the table before it ever happens at the pool.
Reach, throw, don't go. A broom, a wet towel and a bottle on a line all bring teddy in from the edge, and her own feet never leave dry ground.
Her whole name, her street, and a shout that carries. First, middle and last said as one thing, the house number after it, and permission to be as loud as the moment needs.

What holds a thing up and what takes it down. A capped bottle comes back up every time, a filled one stays on the bottom, and a foil boat takes beans one at a time until the water comes over the side.
you: Stillness has to be taught, and one minute is the right dose
Invented powers tell you what she values
Bridging imaginary heroes to real ones is worth doing deliberately
Moral reasoning develops faster through discussion than through rules
Making rules is a different skill from following them
Competence is the most reliable source of confidence

opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 12 months this week. He walks, or he is two weeks off it, drinks from his own cup without help, and follows one instruction at a time, which is why he gets a pitcher at the pool edge and a bucket of his own to tip out. Stay within arm's reach of him every time there is water down.

days.title: What Holds You Up
days.prepTonight: Rinse six empty 500 ml bottles, screw the caps on tight, and stand them by the back door with the tape, the marker and two old towels.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Bottle That Won't Go Under

opening.title: The Bottle That Won't Go Under
opening.need: 2 of the capped bottles · 1 dishpan half filled with water · 1 pitcher of water.
steps: Give her a capped bottle and let her push it under. It comes back up every time, and she will run that ten times before she looks up.
Open the second bottle, fill it from the pitcher, cap it and let her put that one in. It sits on the bottom and stays there.
Ask what is inside the one that keeps coming up. Take her answer, then tip the full one out with her and stand it upside down to drain: teddy needs six bottles of nothing but air at 9:15.

main.title: Teddy's Life Jacket
materials: 6 empty plastic bottles with caps, 500 ml
1 dishpan or deep storage box, filled
1 teddy or plastic doll that can get wet
steps: Spread one towel under the bowl and keep the other within reach. Sit teddy in the water on his own and let her watch him get heavy and go over.
Number the bottles 1 to 6 with the marker so she can count what she has used.
Tape bottle 1 across teddy's back and put him in. Ask whether more of him is out of the water than last time, and let her answer first.
Add one bottle at a time, testing after each. Have her call it first: does this one hold his chin clear, or does he need another?
Stop when his chin stays clear on its own, and count the bottles out loud together.
Unscrew one cap under the water, keeping it closed in your other hand, and let her watch the air leave in bubbles. Teddy drops by that much. Dry him and stand him in the sun.
main.tip: Check every cap is tight before you start. One loose cap fills and teddy goes under.

outside.title: Setting Up the Kiddie Pool
paras: Get the pool onto the flattest patch of grass while the sun is still low. Scrub it with a brush and dish soap, rinse, then let her hold the hose while it fills. June tap water comes out cold and reaches something usable by one o'clock. If the morning stays cool, fill it halfway and top it up with two pans of hot water at half past twelve, stirred right through first.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and on his feet round the pool edge. Give him a small pitcher and one instruction at a time: put it in the pool. He can follow that now, and he will run the trip from tap to pool until you stop him.

second.title: The Starfish Outline
second.intro: The float has a shape, and she learns it on dry ground, where nothing goes near her ears.
materials: A flat patch of patio or path
The kiddie pool, filled that morning, or a deep storage box
1 kitchen timer or a phone timer
steps: Draw a chalk starfish on the patio, five fat arms, wide enough for her to lie inside with room to spare.
She lies in it face up, arms and legs along the arms. Chalk round her own body instead if she would rather.
Teach the head position on the ground: ears down in the chalk, chin up at the sky, tummy pushed up. Count to ten out loud while she holds it.

Move to the pool. Kreston goes in the high chair beside you for the whole ninety minutes; your hands are both under her back. She sits down first, then lies back with your hand flat between her shoulder blades.
Set the timer for one minute and say the seconds out loud. She will sit up four times. Start again from the count she reached.
Take your hand away for two seconds, telling her before you move it every time, and put it straight back.
Wipe her face with the washcloth when she comes up, dry her with one towel, and keep the second for the puddle indoors.
second.tip: Say I am taking my hand away now before you move it, even on the fifth go. Surprise turns a float into a fright.

alternatives: Chalk starfish only, no pool, and float on the lawn.
Race the teddies with their bottles still taped on.
The bowl on a towel indoors, faces in the water only.
outAgain: Meet a friend at the park, and take the chalk
The splash pad, if your town runs one by mid-June
The shady end of the green, if the sun is too much
A walk for popsicles, eaten on a wall

aroundWorld.title: The Netherlands: The Swimming Diploma 🏊
paras: About a quarter of the Netherlands sits below sea level and the country is threaded with canals, so Dutch children swim before they read. Most earn Zwemdiploma A at five or six, and part of that test happens in clothes and shoes, because nobody falls into a canal in a swimsuit.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Make the reward Dutch. Warm a stroopwafel over a mug of tea until the syrup softens, and hand it over after the pool.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Dutch pools hang the diplomas on the wall, and children swim a lap holding one up.

days.krestonPM: He comes out of the high chair once the float is finished. Sit him at the shallow edge in two centimeters of water, you within arm's reach the whole time. At 12 months he drinks from a cup and will try to drink this, so keep a cup of clean water beside you and swap it in each time.

insight.headline: Stillness has to be taught, and one minute is the right dose.
paras: Floating asks Azlyn to hold still while everything in her body says move, and stillness is a skill she is starting to own rather than one she has. Psychologists call it inhibitory control, the same muscle she uses in musical statues and in waiting her turn, and at three it runs in seconds rather than minutes. Counting a minute out loud hands her a shape to hold to and an ending she can hear coming. She will break it. Start again from the count she reached. Short goes across a week build the hold; one long go teaches her that water is where she fails.

days.safety: Standing water. Kreston is 12 months and walking, and a child that age can drown in a few centimeters, in silence, in the dishpan or in the kiddie pool. Tip the bowl out when the Main Event finishes and the pool before evening. From the moment it is filled at half past ten, the back door stays shut and locked and neither of them goes into the yard without you. The two pans of hot water go out at the end of lunch, with Kreston still in the high chair indoors. Pour them in from the far side of the pool and stir, then hold a whole hand in the water before Azlyn gets near it. Sunscreen on both of them before you go out, and again after the water. The caps are the second hazard: six loose 500 ml caps in a room with a 12-month-old is a choking risk. Count them out at the start and back at the end, and the one you unscrew in step 6 stays in your hand.

days.title: The Water Powers
days.prepTonight: Poke six holes in the bottom of one plastic cup with a skewer, stand it by the back door with two whole cups, and put the straws and the ball on the table.

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Farm Animals on the Rug

opening.title: The Powers She Gives Herself
steps: Ask what powers she would want in water. Write each one across the top of the page in her own words, wrong grammar and all.
She draws herself using the one she likes best. Gills, a tail, floating above the sea.
Tell her that one power on her list is real and she has it. Do not say which. It waits until 9:15.

main.title: The Bubble Breath Test
materials: 1 ping-pong ball, or a plastic bottle cap instead
steps: Bowl of warm water on the table, hand towel beside it, tissue scrap in front of her. Prop the mirror where she can see her own face.
Blow the tissue across the table, first with a huge puff, then with the smallest breath that still shifts it. Her breath is the power on her list.
Float the ball in the bowl and blow it from one side to the other. Then race, one of you at each end, one breath each.
Straws out, one each. Blow at the ball through a straw so she feels the thinner, faster stream. Then straw under the water, bubbles, and count how long she keeps one string going.
Last game: chin resting on the water, mouth under, hum out. Do it yourself first and let her watch your face.
Stop the moment she coughs. Hand her the towel and let her say whether there is another go in it.
main.tip: Let her choose when her mouth goes in. She might do it in the first minute or take three days. Push her and the three days become two weeks.

outside.title: The Hose Rainbow
paras: Stand with the sun behind you, thumb half over the end of the hose, and send a fine spray across the grass. The June sun sits high at eleven, so aim the spray downwards and look for the bow low, lying on the grass in front of your own shadow rather than up in the air. Hand her the hose and let her hunt for the angle that keeps it there. No sun means no bow, and the fine spray still works on its own, with her walking through her own rain.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and walking. Sit him on the dry grass at the edge of the spray so the mist reaches him rather than the water. He will pat the wet grass, look at his hand, and pat it again. Give him one instruction at a time: touch the water.

second.title: The Sponge Pump
second.intro: Same water, four tools, one job: get the full bowl into the empty one.
materials: 1 turkey baster, or a clean squeezy sauce bottle instead
3 plastic cups, one with holes poked in the bottom
steps: Set the two bowls at opposite ends of the tray on the patio. Fill one from the pitcher and leave the other empty.
Sponge first. Soak it, lift it dripping, squeeze it out over the empty bowl. Let her run that five or six times without commentary.
Hand her the baster and show the order once: squeeze, then in, then let go. She will get it backwards twice before it sticks.
Fill all three cups from the pitcher. Two hold and one leaks, so the leaking one has to be carried faster than it empties.
Ask which tool moved the most water. Take her answer, then test it. Empty everything back and give each tool one minute.
Pour the last of the pitcher from up high, then from low down, and let her hold a hand in the stream both times.
Tip both bowls out onto the grass, wipe the tray, and dry her hands and feet on the towels.
second.tip: Do this in swimwear or in nothing at all. Every version ends with her sitting down in the full bowl.

alternatives: Sponge and one bucket on the grass, nothing else.
Wash the doll's clothes and clip them on the line.
The baster and a tray of colored water indoors.
outAgain: The farm, and find the trough, the tap and the water pump
The duck pond, with oats rather than bread
The garden center, for the watering cans
A friend's kiddie pool, if anyone else has one out
days.krestonPM: He stays in the stroller wherever the animals are and gets his own feet on the path between the barns, where at 12 months he will walk four steps and then want carrying. Wash both sets of hands before the snack comes out.

insight.headline: Invented powers tell you what she values.
paras: Ask Azlyn for a superpower and you get a clean read on what she wishes she had more of. Three-year-olds pick powers that fix the size of the world: being tall enough, being fast, breathing underwater, never having to come inside. Her list this morning records what she has noticed about her own limits. Keep the page and put the date on it. The powers she picks at four will be different ones, and the change is the part worth having. Ask her again in September, after a summer of getting in the water. Read the old list back to her when you do, and the year shows up in what she has stopped wishing for.

days.safety: Never push her face toward the water and never hold her there. Stop the second she coughs, because forced breath-holding teaches fear and nothing else. Wet patio slabs are slippery under bare feet, so keep the running on the grass. Kreston is in the high chair beside you for the whole of the sponge pump, because two full dishpans and a new walker do not share a patio. Sunscreen on both of them before you go out, and again after the water. Both bowls get tipped out before you leave for the farm, not when you get back. At the farm, hands get washed with soap and water on the way out of every animal area and before anything is eaten. Hand gel is not enough on a farm. No food or drink goes into the barns, and Kreston stays in the stroller wherever the animals are.

days.title: The Lifeguard
days.prepTonight: Find the whistle and tie a wool loop through it to fit her wrist, or settle on the word you will shout instead, and stand the red towel, the tape, the chalk and the clipboard by the back door.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Whistle and What It Means

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Chalk Pool on the Path

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Pool That Opens at One O'Clock

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Two Books in the Cool Room

opening.title: The Whistle and What It Means
opening.need: 1 whistle, or one word you both agree to shout · everyone who is in the house.
steps: Blow it once, at the table, over breakfast. Let the shock of it land.
Agree what it means: everybody stops and looks at whoever blew it. One whistle, one rule.
Practice on the household. She blows, everyone freezes, including you. Six goes and she owns it.

main.title: The Lifeguard Chair
materials: 1 dining chair, the sturdiest in the house
Paper and a bulldog clip as a clipboard
1 whistle on a loop of wool sized for her wrist, or a chosen shout word instead
steps: Stand the chair on level floor, all four legs down, nothing underneath. Press hard on the seat and on each front corner, and check it does not rock before she gets up.
Roll the red towel tight along its length and tape both ends. That is the float.
Clip paper into the bulldog clip and write LIFEGUARD across the top in marker. She fills the rest with whatever counts as writing today.
Sun hat on, whistle on the wool loop round her wrist, float on her lap. Sit her up and let her look at the room for a minute before you say anything.
Give her the job in one sentence: watch the water, blow the whistle if anybody needs help. Then run three drills with a teddy in trouble.
Ask what a lifeguard does when nothing is going wrong. Sitting still and watching is most of the job.
main.tip: Take a turn in the chair yourself and let her be the swimmer who ignores every rule.

outside.title: The Chalk Pool on the Path
paras: Draw a pool on the path in chalk, big enough to lie down in, with a deep end, a shallow end and lane lines down the middle. Walk the outline together, then chalk an arrow at the deep end pointing to the grass where the chair stands this afternoon.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and walking with a hand held. Give him a cup of water and a fat paintbrush and let him paint the paving, where every mark fades in the sun.

second.title: The Pool That Opens at One O'Clock
second.intro: The chalk pool opens for business at one.
materials: The chalk pool from this morning
The lifeguard chair and rolled-towel float
Chalk, 2 or 3 fat sticks, for the rules by the entrance
1 pitcher of water and cups for the pool cafe
Sun hats, and shade to move into
steps: She cuts a stack of tickets with the child-safe scissors while you sit alongside. Rough rectangles, ten or so, and she decides the price.
Chalk three rules by the entrance in her words, and add the one you care about: no hat, no ticket.
Carry the chair to the grass the arrow points at and press it down until all four legs bed in level. Lay the two towels at the pool edge for sunbathing, and open the doors.
The teddies line, pay and swim. She takes the chair with the float across her knees.
Every few minutes, put a teddy in trouble at the deep end. She whistles, calls the rule, and throws the float. Let her miss and throw again.
Run the cafe from the pitcher and cups. She pours for every customer, and the pool shuts for twenty minutes while everyone drinks in the shade.
Closing time at half past two. One whistle, everybody out, towels in, and the chair comes back to the kitchen.
second.tip: Stay a customer. The moment you start running the pool it becomes your game.

alternatives: Tickets and a cafe, no pool, at the kitchen table in the cool.
The lifeguard chair indoors, watching over a bowl of water.
Teddy goes in the bath and she teaches him the five tests instead.
outAgain: A sunset walk, the afternoon version of it, once the paving has cooled
The river path, for water she cannot get into
The park with the shade trees and a picnic blanket
The garden with the sprinkler on and nowhere to be
days.krestonPM: He is the paying customer. Hand him a ticket at 12 months and he will hand it straight back, then take it again. He is playing that game with everything this month. Keep him in the shade with his own cup, which he drinks from without help now.

insight.headline: Bridging imaginary heroes to real ones is worth doing deliberately.
paras: Azlyn spends a lot of her play as somebody with powers, and a lifeguard sits at the join between that and the world. The job comes with a chair, a whistle and a rule she can name, and it belongs to a person she will see at the pool on Tuesday. Pretending to be one is how she tries the role on from the inside, and a rule she has enforced herself lands harder than one she has been told. On Tuesday, point the real one out and say what she has in common with him. A person she can find again holds the idea steady in a way an invented one never manages.

days.safety: The chair. A dining chair seat puts her head above your chest, and a three-year-old who stands up on one or leans out for a teddy goes down head first. Nothing goes under the legs to raise it, she sits rather than stands, the chair goes on grass rather than on the paving, and she is never up there while you are indoors. When you leave the garden, the chair comes with you. Nothing goes round her neck while she is up there, so the whistle rides on a wool loop round her wrist. Mid-June sun is the other one. The path gets hot enough to hurt bare feet by one o'clock, and a 12-month-old overheats faster than she does, so sun hats on both of them, sunscreen before you go out and again after the water, shade to move into, and the pitcher going round every twenty minutes. Keep Kreston out of direct sun altogether.

days.title: Reach, Don't Go
days.prepTonight: Cut two meters off the clothesline, tie one end round the neck of the empty 2 L bottle, and leave it with the broom by the back door.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Teddy in the Deep End

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Water Map of the Street

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Her Name and Her Loud Voice

opening.title: Hunting for the Longest Thing
opening.need: the house · a clear strip of hallway floor.
steps: Send her to find the longest thing she can carry. She comes back with a broom, a towel, a belt, an umbrella.
Lay them end to end down the hall and put her flat on the floor beside them. Sort them into the ones longer than her and the ones shorter.
Stand the longest three by the back door and tell her teddy will need them.

main.title: The Teddy in the Deep End
materials: The kiddie pool or a deep storage box, filled
1 teddy that can get wet, or a capped bottle with a face drawn on
1 large towel to throw and pull
steps: Float teddy out in the middle, past her arms. Give her the rule first: she stays out, and she stays dry. Kreston goes in the high chair beside you for the whole hour, because a filled pool and a new walker do not share a patio.
Broom first. She kneels at the edge, holds the end, and works teddy in with the handle. Say the words with her: reach, don't go.
Towel next. She throws one end out, keeps hold of the other, and drags. It works better wet.
Now the line. She throws the bottle past teddy and pulls it back so it sweeps him in on the way.
Move teddy further out after each rescue until nothing reaches. Ask what she does then, and give her the answer: shout for a grown-up.
Untie the line from the bottle and put the string away in the drawer while she watches.
main.tip: Run the whole hour on the same three words. Reach, throw, don't go. She will chant it back at you by the fourth rescue.

outside.title: The Water Map of the Street
paras: Walk the street with a scrap of card and a marker and mark every place water sits: the drains, the rain barrel, the neighbor's pond, the puddle that never dries out by the wall. You hold her hand for the whole time you are at the pond, both of you well back from the edge, and Kreston stays in the stroller there. Count them at the gate on the way home. June has dried most of it up.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and stops at every drain on the street, because a hole with a sound coming out of it is the best thing out there. Let him crouch and look. He will point at it and then check your face to see that you saw it too.

second.title: Her Name and Her Loud Voice
second.intro: Reaching handles teddy. The other half of the drill is the noise she makes when nothing reaches.
materials: 1 sheet of thick card or a flattened cereal box
An old phone or a toy phone
A photo of the front of the house (optional)
steps: Go into the yard and shout first yourself, full volume: HELP! I NEED A GROWN-UP! Then her, three times, louder each go.
Teach the whole name. First, middle, last, said as one thing. Chant it, sing it, clap it out.
Add the street. Say your house number and street name together until she gives it back without a prompt.
Play the questions game with the old phone. You ring, she answers, you ask her name and where she lives. Swap over and let her ring you.
Card time. She draws the front of the house, or tapes the photo on, and you write her full name, the address and your number underneath in marker.
Tape the card up by the phone at her eye height and read it back together twice.
Ask her the two questions again at bedtime, and again tomorrow at breakfast. It takes a week of asking.
second.tip: Give her the loud voice as a job with permission attached. After three years of quiet indoors, she needs telling out loud that this shout is allowed.

alternatives: Name and address only, chanted on a walk.
Draw the house and stop there.
Ring Grandma and let her say her whole name.
Practice the shout in the yard and go back in.
outAgain: The hill walk, and count the water she can see from the top
The shady woods loop if the hill is too hot
The park, for the swings and nothing else
A slow walk with the water map, adding whatever she missed
The stream at the bottom of the hill, held by the hand
days.krestonPM: He goes up the hill in the carrier and does the flat top on his own feet. At 12 months walking on grass is harder than walking on carpet, so expect him to sit down every few steps. Give him one job at the top: hold his own water cup, wider than his mouth. He will carry it home.

insight.headline: Pretend urgency produces real problem-solving.
paras: A frightened three-year-old cannot look up a plan. Under real stress Azlyn loses the words and freezes, which is what most adults do until training has replaced the thinking. Rehearsal is how the sequence gets in: the broom, the throw, the shout, run in a game where teddy is the one in trouble and nobody is scared. She practices the movement and the words in the same minute, the broom in her hands while her mouth says reach, don't go, so the two come back attached to each other. Run it again in two weeks without warning her, and again in the summer. The rescue she does on the third go is the one still there in a year.

days.safety: Practice reaching at the kiddie pool only. Never rehearse this at a pond, a canal or a river edge, where a wet bank and a leaning three-year-old go in together. Her hand stays in yours at the neighbor's pond this morning, and Kreston stays in the stroller. The throw line comes down and goes away the moment you finish, because a loop of string at Kreston's height is a strangulation risk. Sunscreen on both of them before you go out, and again after the water. Tip the pool out before you leave for the hill. The pool stays filled until half past two, so Kreston is in the high chair on the step or indoors with the back door shut for the whole of that stretch, and never in the yard while there is water down.

days.title: Talk, Then Swim
days.prepTonight: Cut fourteen cards out of a flattened cereal box with the kitchen scissors and leave them on the table with the crayons and the marker.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Four Places With Water In Them

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Swim Bag She Packs Herself

opening.title: Four Places With Water In Them
opening.need: 4 of the cut cards · crayons · 1 marker.
steps: Ask her to name four places that have water in them. She will give you the bath and the pool without thinking, then stall. Wait her out.
One place per card, drawn by her. Write the name across the top of each in marker while she works.
Lay the four in a row on the table and leave them there. They are the map for 9:15.

main.title: The What-If Pile
materials: 8–10 cards cut from a cereal box (cut last night, or torn into rough rectangles at the table now)
The four place cards from this morning
steps: Lay the four place cards out and put the blank pile beside them.
Read one out. You are at the pond and your ball is in the water. What do you do? Take whatever she says.
Write her answer on a card in her exact words, wrong ones included, and let her draw a small picture on it so she can find it again. Put the card under the place it belongs to.
Keep going through six or seven. The ball in the pond, the open gate, losing you at the pool, a big kid pushing, teddy in the deep end.
Where an answer worries you, hand the two teddies over and let one of them try her plan out rather than correcting her.
Read the whole pile back at the end. She can change any card she wants, and you rewrite it as she says it.
main.tip: Ask and then what happens? instead of steering. She hears her own answer run to the end and fixes it herself.

outside.title: Hunting for the Cold Spot
paras: Mid-June and hot by eleven, so go out and find the cold. Turn the outside tap on and let her hold a hand under it. The first of it comes out warm off the standing pipe, then it turns cold enough that she pulls her hand back, and that switch is the whole point. Fill a cup and take it round the block. She holds it against her cheek at the gate, at the corner and on the doorstep, and tells you when it stops being cold. Hats and sunscreen on both of them before you open the door, and she drinks the cup on the doorstep.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months. Hold his hand under the tap for two seconds and let his face do the whole report. Sunscreen on him before he goes out. Then sit him in the shade with a cup of his own to tip and fill again, and keep him off the sunny paving between eleven and three.

second.title: The Swim Bag She Packs Herself
second.intro: Pool day. She owns the bag from now on, and the packing takes as long as it takes.
materials: Paper and crayons for the picture list
A snack and a drink for after
steps: Make the picture list first. She draws one thing per line: swimsuit, towel, snack, drink, diaper. You write the word beside each drawing.
She fetches each item and lays it on the floor next to its picture. Nothing goes in the bag until the row is complete.
Practice the swimsuit. In, out, in again, standing on her towel, no help offered unless she asks twice.
Kreston's diaper and towel go in their own end of the bag, packed by her, so she knows where they are when you have both hands full.
Load the bag against the list, and let her put the snack and the drink in last so they come out first.
Clip the picture list to the bag handle. It comes home again for next week.
Bag by the front door by two o'clock, and she carries it out.
second.tip: Let her pack something daft alongside the sensible things. A bag she packed herself is one she keeps packing at four, at six and at nine.

alternatives: Picture list only, and you pack the bag.
Practice the swimsuit and skip the list.
Pack the bag for a teddy going swimming.
Draw the pool from memory: doors, water, the big clock.
outAgain: Swimming, and she gets in with the what-if pile already in her
The pool café afterwards, for the window over the water
A shady park on the way home if there is anything left in her
Straight home and the kiddie pool, if the pool is booked out
Indoor playground, on a day too hot for anywhere without a fan
days.krestonPM: He swims too. At 12 months he holds on to you with his whole body, so go chest to chest and face to face for the first few minutes. Blow a light breath across his face before anything splashes it, which gives him the reflex to shut his eyes. Twenty minutes and out; he gets cold well before she does.

insight.headline: Moral reasoning develops faster through discussion than through rules.
paras: A rule covers the situation you thought of. Azlyn meets the pond you never mentioned, and a child who has only been handed rules has nothing to work from. Talking it through gives her the working. She runs the problem, hears her own answer out loud, and follows it to the end while you say and then what happens? Reasoning it out with her leaves her holding a judgment that travels to the next situation, and it holds longer than a rule does. Writing her answers down in her own words is what makes it hers. The pile on the table is her thinking, and she knows it.

days.safety: At the pool, armbands, rings and float suits are toys. Treat them as toys, because a child can slip under one without a sound. Both of them stay inside arm's reach in the water, close enough to take hold of without a step. Poolside tiles and the changing room floor are the slipperiest surfaces either of them will meet this week, so walk it and hold hands, both ways.

days.title: The Rules Sign
days.prepTonight: Flatten a big cereal box or find a large sheet of card, and put it on the table with the marker, the crayons and the tape.

opening.title: The Rules She Already Knows
steps: Ask her what the water rules in this house already are, rather than what they ought to be.
Write down every one she gives you, including no weeing in the pool and anything else that arrives. Do not edit as you go.
Read the list back and let her pick the five that matter most. Star those five. They go on the sign at 9:15.

main.title: Five Rules on One Sign
materials: 1 large sheet of card or a flattened cereal box
steps: Rule the card into five boxes with the marker, or fold it into five and open it out again. Number the boxes 1 to 5 with her.
Take rule one off the starred list and ask her how to draw it. Follow her design, even where a stick figure ends up in a pool the size of a sock.
She draws all five in crayon. You write the words underneath each one in marker, in her wording, with her name at the bottom.
She signs it. A scribble, an A, a handprint in crayon, whatever she calls a signature this month.
Tape it up by the back door at her eye height, where she passes it on the way to the pool.
Walk her past it and let her read all five back to you from the pictures. She can.
main.tip: Write her words as she said them. Don't go in without a grown-up survives being read out by a three-year-old; Adult supervision required does not.

outside.title: Tipping Out the Buckets
paras: Walk the garden and empty everything holding water: the buckets, the watering can, the trays under the pots, the wheelbarrow, the lid of the rain barrel, the kiddie pool. Tell her why while she tips. A week of June sun on standing water gives you mosquitoes, and the tipping is now part of her job at the end of every water day.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months. Give him the smallest empty bucket and one instruction: tip it out. He can follow that now, and he will tip it out over his own feet the first time. Let him carry the empty bucket around the yard after you, a trick two weeks old and one he is proud of.

second.title: How Many Before It Sinks
second.intro: Foil, water, and a pile of beans. She finds out how much a boat carries by sinking it.
materials: 1 dishpan or deep tray of water
Dried beans or coins, a handful
1 pot or lidded jar to keep the beans in
Paper and a marker for the tally
steps: Tear six squares of foil off the roll. Set the bowl of water on the table with the dish towel under it.
She shapes the first boat however she wants. You make two more: one flat as a raft, one pinched up into a deep cup.
Float boat one and load beans in one at a time. Count out loud together and stop counting when the water comes over the side.
Write the number on the tally sheet next to a quick drawing of that boat shape.
Run the raft and the deep cup the same way. Same beans, same counting, numbers on the same sheet.
Compare the three numbers with her. Then squeeze one boat into a tight ball and drop it in, and let her watch the same foil go straight down.
Count every bean back into the pot out loud, and dry hands and table with the dish towel.
second.tip: She will want to load them in by the fistful. Hold the one-at-a-time rule for the first two boats so the numbers mean something, then let the third one go however she likes.

alternatives: Two boats, no tally, and stop when she stops.
Float what the kitchen offers: a lid, a cork, a spoon, an apple.
Build a foil boat for a clothespin doll and sail it in the sink.
Draw boats instead, and count who is on board.
outAgain: Indoor playground, the quiet session, when the big ones are still at school
The library, if you would rather sit down
The park at four, once the slide has come out of the sun
A cold drink somewhere with a fan
The shady half of the woods loop
days.krestonPM: Indoor playground at the quiet hour is his session more than hers. At 12 months he pulls up on the padded blocks and walks the soft uneven floor, which asks more of his ankles than the kitchen floor does. Keep him in the under-twos area. Let Azlyn show him one thing and then leave them to it.

insight.headline: Making rules is a different skill from following them.
paras: Following a rule asks Azlyn to remember. Making one asks her to work out what goes wrong and who it goes wrong for, which is a harder job and a more useful one. A rule she helped write is one she keeps, and she will enforce it on everybody in the house, including you, with more conviction than you would like. That is authorship doing its work. She wrote these five and drew them, and the sign by the door belongs to her. Send her to it when somebody forgets a rule, and let her be the one who reads it out.

days.safety: Dried beans and coins are a choking hazard, and they will end up on the floor with a walking 12-month-old in the room. Count them out, count them back, and sweep before you put him down. The tray of water stays on the table, never on the floor. Sunscreen on both of them before the garden round, and again after any water.

days.title: The Diploma
days.prepTonight: Cut five cards from a cereal box and stand them by the crayons with the whistle and the timer. The pool gets filled after breakfast, not tonight.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Five Things She Can Do

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Five Tests in the Kiddie Pool

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: Her Turn to Ask the Questions

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Week, Told in the Bath

opening.title: The Five Things She Can Do
opening.need: 5 cards cut last night · crayons · 1 marker.
steps: Ask what she can do in water now that she could not last Friday. Hand the week back if she stalls: the bottles, the starfish, the whistle, the broom, the shout.
Five of them, one per card, drawn by her. Write each one across the top in marker in her words.
She lays the cards in the order she wants, and draws an empty box in the corner of each for the tick.

main.title: The Five Tests in the Kiddie Pool
materials: The kiddie pool, or a deep storage box, filled while she has breakfast
1 whistle on its wool loop, or the shout word instead
1 empty capped 2 L bottle on a short line
The five cards from this morning
steps: Fill the pool while she has her breakfast, and lay the five cards on a towel at the pool edge with the timer beside them. Straight from the tap it will be cold at quarter past nine, so tell her before her feet go in and keep the run inside twenty minutes. Describe every test as you come to it.
The float. She lies back with your hand under her back, ears down, chin up, and the timer runs for one minute. Tick the card.
The bubbles. Chin on the water, mouth under, hum out for a count of ten. Tick the card.
The reach. Teddy goes out past her arms. She throws the bottle beyond him and pulls it back so it sweeps him in, feet staying out. Tick the card.
The shout, then the whistle. She calls her whole name and HELP loud enough for next door. Then, while she plays, blow the whistle once: she stops dead and comes to the edge. Two ticks.
Out, dry with the other two towels, put the line and the whistle away, and let her carry the five ticked cards inside.
main.tip: Tick the card the moment each test ends, in front of her. She will watch your pen harder than she watched the water.

outside.title: Washing the Wheels
paras: Tip the pool out onto the lawn and keep a bucket of it back for the wheels. Sponge down the stroller wheels, her trike, the bin wheels and the bottom of the back gate. Wheels are filthy by June and nobody washes them.

days.infant: Kreston is 12 months and copying what he sees your hands do. Give him a wet washcloth and a dry wheel of his own, because a sponge comes apart in a mouth. He will chew it, then wipe, then chew it again. Wringing a full cloth takes more grip than he has, so wring it out for him and hand it back damp.

second.title: The Diploma She Signs Herself
second.intro: Five ticked cards turn into one thing that goes on the fridge and stays there.
materials: 1 sheet of thick card or a cereal box
A printed photo from the week, or your phone
steps: Write DIPLOMA across the top in marker, big. She copies the letters underneath if she wants.
She draws herself in the water in the middle of the card. Give her the space and leave her to it.
Take the five cards one at a time and ask what that one says. Write her sentence on the diploma: I can float for one minute. Her words, five lines.
Look back through the week's photos while she works, or tape the printed one into a corner.
She signs the bottom. You write the date beside it and sign under her.
Read the five lines out loud to whoever is in the house, then let her read them to Kreston.
Fridge, magnet or tape, at her height. It stays up until she takes it down.
second.tip: Read the lines as facts rather than praise. You can float for one minute does something well done, clever girl cannot.

alternatives: One line and a drawing, no ceremony.
Make a diploma for Kreston too, for getting in the water at all.
Draw the whole week as a comic strip, one box per day.
outAgain: The pharmacy, for the sunscreen, and the park bench afterwards
The shady playground, and the ice cream van if it is there
A slow loop of the block with the trike she washed
The library garden, if the reading corner is too warm
days.krestonPM: He stays in the stroller in the pharmacy and comes out for the bench. At 12 months he wants down the second the wheels stop, so pick the bench by grass rather than by the road. Give him the sun hat to carry and a cup of water on the bench.

insight.headline: Competence is the most reliable source of confidence.
paras: Confidence at three grows out of evidence. Azlyn now has five things she can name and do in water, and she collected them across seven days, which is worth more than a week of being told she is brave. Psychologists call these mastery experiences, and they are the strongest source of a child's belief in what she can do. The diploma holds the evidence still, and she will point at it in November. Keep it on the fridge until it goes yellow, and add the next five underneath when they arrive. Read the five lines back to her on the next day she decides she cannot do something.

days.safety: The pool is full from breakfast until you tip it out at half past ten, and this is the day you stop noticing it. It gets filled in the morning, never overnight, because a pool left standing is the one thing Wednesday taught her to empty. Kreston can climb into a kiddie pool on his own now and cannot get himself out. The back door stays shut and locked whenever you are not out there with them, you stay within arm's reach of both while the tests run, and the tipping out happens at half past ten. Sunscreen on both of them before you go out and again after the water, and the whistle stays on its wool loop round her wrist rather than round her neck.
